questions.text:
A relational database contains two tables Student and Performance as shown below:

The primary key of the Student table is Roll_no. For the Performance table, the columns Roll_no. and Subject_code together from the primary key. Consider the SQL query given below: 
SELECT S.Student_name, sum(P.Marks)
FROM Student S, Performance P
WHERE  P.Marks  >  84
GROUP BY S.Student_name;
The number of rows returned by the above SQL query is _________ .
questions.solution:
There is no join condition, so FROM makes a cross product: every student is paired with every Performance row.

WHERE Marks [latex]\gt[/latex] 84 keeps the 5 performance rows with marks 86, 95, 90, 89, 92, and each is paired with all 5 students.

GROUP BY Student_name gives one row per student name [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 rows.

Answer: 5

questions.text:
Let the set of functional dependencies [latex]F=\{QR\rightarrow S,R\rightarrow P,S\rightarrow Q\}[/latex] hold on a relation schema X = (PQRS). X is not in BCNF. Suppose X is decomposed into two schemas Y and Z where Y = (PR) and Z = (QRS).
Consider the two statements given below:

I. Both Y and Z are in BCNF
II. Decomposition of X into Y and Z is dependency preserving and lossless.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Y(P, R): R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P with R as key [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] BCNF.
- Z(Q, R, S): QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q. Keys are QR and RS. In S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q, S is not a superkey [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Z is not BCNF. So I is false.
- Dependencies: R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is in Y; QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q are in Z [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] preserved.
- Lossless: common attribute R, and R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P makes R a key of Y [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] lossless. So II is true.

Answer: II only

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct about the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree data structure used for creating an index of a relational database table?
questions.solution:
In a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree only the leaf nodes hold pointers to data records. Non-leaf nodes contain only keys and pointers to child nodes.

The other statements are true (height balanced, sorted keys, leaves linked).

Answer: Non-leaf nodes have pointers to data records

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Non-leaf nodes have pointers to data records
Key values in each node are kept in sorted order
Each leaf node has a pointer to the next leaf node

questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about database transaction schedules:

I. Strict two-phase locking protocol generates conflict serializable schedules that are also recoverable.
II. Timestamp-ordering concurrency control protocol with Thomas' Write Rule can generate view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit, so schedules are conflict serializable and no transaction reads uncommitted data [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] recoverable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete writes, which allows some view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable (blind writes) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both I and II

questions.text:
Let us assume that transaction T1 has arrived before transaction T2. Consider the schedule s=r1(A);r2(B):w2(A);w1(B)
Which of the following is true?
questions.solution:
TS(T1) [latex]\lt[/latex] TS(T2).
- r1(A): RTS(A) = T1. r2(B): RTS(B) = T2.
- w2(A): T2 is not older than A's reader [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] allowed.
- w1(B): B was already read by the younger T2 (RTS(B) = T2 [latex]\gt[/latex] TS(T1)) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1 is rolled back.

Answer: Not allowed under basic timestamp protocols because T1 is rolled back

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Not allowed under basic timestamp protocols because T1 is rolled back.
Not allowed under basic timestamp protocols because T2 is rolled back.
